subject: Creativity
title: Intellectual Property: How Ideas Become Assets
description: A micro-lesson that makes Intellectual Property: How Ideas Become Assets usable.

hook.text: Mickey Mouse has generated over $80 billion for Disney. Not the theme parks. Not the movies.

buildup.text: Intellectual property (IP) — patents, copyrights, trademarks, trade secrets — turns intangible ideas into legally.

discovery.text: IP now accounts for 90% of the S&P 500's market value, up from 17% in 1975.

twist.text: Coca-Cola's formula is a trade secret, never patented — because patents expire after 20 years.

climax.text: In the creative economy, understanding IP is as important as the creative work itself.

punchline.text: In the creative economy, owning the idea matters more than making the product.

quiz.question: What percentage of S&P 500 market value does IP now account for?

details.summary: Intellectual property transforms intangible creative work into legally protected economic assets through patents, copyrights, trademarks, and trade secrets. These protections give creators ownership of their ideas and the ability to monetize them through licensing, sales, and enforcement.
details.whyItMatters: IP law determines who profits from creative work. Understanding IP is essential for any creator because it defines ownership, controls distribution, and generates revenue long after the original work is complete.
takeaways: Copyright protects creative expression automatically upon creation
Patents protect inventions and require formal application
IP can generate revenue for decades through licensing and royalties

faq.question: What is the difference between copyright and patent?
faq.answer: Copyright protects creative expression like writing, music, and art automatically when created. Patents protect functional inventions and processes, requiring formal application and approval. Both provide time-limited monopolies but cover fundamentally different types of creative output.

faq.question: Do you need to register copyright?
faq.answer: In most countries, copyright exists automatically when a work is created in tangible form. Registration provides additional legal advantages in infringement disputes, including the ability to claim statutory damages in the United States. Registration is recommended but not required.
